chapters.title: Chapter 6: Portfolio and Capital Allocation Across Regimes

lessons.title: Risk Budgeting Across Multiple Systematic Strategies

body.text: Four strategies, each independently computing its own regime-aware position size, can in aggregate ask for more risk than the book actually has room for, especially when their risks are not nearly as independent as summing them assumes.

children.text: Lessons 1 and 2 built regime-aware sizing for a single strategy. Chapter 5's compatibility matrix hands weights to four strategies at once. This lesson addresses what happens when you actually run all four with shared capital and genuinely correlated risk, not the tidy, independent risk each strategy's own sizing formula implicitly assumes.
The Naive Approach: Just Sum the Position Sizes

The simplest, wrong approach is to size each strategy independently using Lesson 1 and 2's methods, then simply add up the resulting risk. This either assumes the strategies' risks are perfectly independent, understating true risk if they are correlated, or it assumes they move in lockstep, overstating risk if they genuinely diversify each other. Neither assumption is checked against reality, and the true answer depends entirely on the actual correlation between the strategies' returns.
Portfolio Variance: The Correct Way to Combine Strategy Risk

body.caption: Portfolio variance across strategies: each pair's weighted, correlation-adjusted covariance, summed over every pair

children.text: When two strategies are uncorrelated, rho equals 0 and their risks partially diversify away. When they move in lockstep, rho equals 1 and risk simply adds, no diversification benefit at all. When they move in opposite directions, a negative rho, combining them can reduce total risk below either strategy alone.
A Worked Example: Momentum and Vol Buying During a Panic

From Chapter 5's compatibility matrix, a Panic Selloff regime weights momentum at 0.70 and vol buying at 0.90. Suppose momentum's own daily volatility is 1.5% and vol buying's is 2.0%, and, since both strategies tend to profit from and be exposed to the same sharp down move during a genuine panic, their return correlation runs elevated at 0.60.

body.caption: Three ways to estimate combined risk for the same two strategies

body.text: The true portfolio volatility, 2.57%, sits between the two naive extremes, closer to the linear-sum estimate than to the independence estimate, exactly because the real correlation (0.60) sits closer to 1 than to 0. Neither naive shortcut gets this right. The independence assumption is the more dangerous of the two errors, because it understates true risk, and it does so most badly in precisely the regimes where strategy correlations tend to spike.

children.text: The Regime Twist: Correlation Itself Is Regime-Dependent

The 0.60 correlation used above is not a fixed constant any more than a single GARCH parameter or a single Kelly fraction is. Chapter 1's correlation dimension established that asset correlations spike sharply during crises; strategy correlations behave the same way, for the same underlying reason. A risk budget built using a calm-period strategy correlation, when strategies genuinely do move more independently of each other, will badly understate true portfolio risk exactly when a real panic hits and those correlations converge, the same failure mode as every other fixed-parameter method this course has examined, now showing up one level higher, at the strategy level rather than the asset level.

body.text: Never estimate strategy correlations from a single, unconditional historical sample and treat the result as fixed. Estimate them per regime, the same discipline Chapters 3 and 4 applied to volatility itself, and budget risk using the correlation appropriate to the regime you are actually entering, not the regime your correlation estimate happened to be measured in.

body.title: Risk Budgeted at a Calm-Period Correlation
body.prompt: Using the same weights (0.70, 0.90) and volatilities (1.5%, 2.0%) as the worked example, but a calm-period correlation estimate of 0.30 instead of the panic-period 0.60, what is the portfolio volatility? Use the portfolio variance formula and take the square root.
body.explanation: sigma-squared = 0.70² × 1.5² + 0.90² × 2.0² + 2 × 0.70 × 0.90 × 1.5 × 2.0 × 0.30 = 1.1025 + 3.24 + 1.134 = 5.4765. Square root ≈ 2.34%. A risk desk that budgeted using this calm-period correlation, then faced an actual panic where correlation jumped to 0.60, would have been under-provisioned by roughly 0.23 percentage points of daily volatility, 2.57% actual versus 2.34% budgeted, right when it mattered most.

body.title: Why Independence Is the More Dangerous Assumption
body.question: Between assuming zero correlation and assuming perfect correlation across strategies, why is the zero-correlation (independence) assumption generally considered the more dangerous error for risk management?
options: It is more dangerous because it always overstates risk, leading to unnecessarily small positions
It is more dangerous because it understates true risk, and correlations tend to rise exactly during the stress regimes where an underestimate of risk is most costly
It is not actually dangerous; both assumptions are equally safe defaults
It is dangerous only for options strategies, not for directional strategies like momentum
body.explanation: Assuming independence produces the lowest possible portfolio volatility estimate for any given set of individual strategy volatilities, which means it understates true risk whenever any real correlation exists. Since correlations across both assets and strategies tend to rise specifically during stress regimes, an independence assumption fails most badly exactly when the cost of underestimating risk is highest.

points: Summing independently-sized strategy positions implicitly assumes a correlation of either 0 or 1, neither of which is checked against the strategies' actual behavior
Portfolio variance, sigma_portfolio-squared = sum over i,j of w_i w_j sigma_i sigma_j rho_ij, is the correct way to combine multiple strategies' risk

In this lesson's worked example, the true portfolio volatility (2.57%) sat between the naive independence estimate (2.08%) and the naive linear-sum estimate (2.85%), closer to the linear-sum side because the actual correlation (0.60) was closer to 1 than to 0
The independence assumption is the more dangerous of the two naive errors, since it understates risk, and understates it most severely exactly when stress-driven correlation spikes matter most
Strategy correlations are themselves regime-dependent, exactly like asset correlations in Chapter 1, and should be estimated per regime rather than treated as a single fixed constant
